draft.title: Introductions, topic sentences and conclusions
card: Introduction
It comes first and tells readers what the text is about and what is coming. It gets readers ready for the ideas that follow.
Topic sentence
It opens a paragraph and states the main idea of that paragraph. The other sentences in the paragraph then give details that support it.
Conclusion
It comes last and draws the ideas together. It reminds readers of the main points and does not start a new one.
Read together, the introduction, topic sentences and conclusion give a text a clear path from start to finish.
draft.remember: Introduction: what is coming. Topic sentence: the paragraph's main idea. Conclusion: ideas drawn together.

a.q: What is the job of a topic sentence in a paragraph?
opts: It states the main idea of the paragraph
It sums up the whole text for the reader
It tells readers what the whole text will cover
It adds a new idea at the end of the text
a.why: A topic sentence opens a paragraph and names its main idea, so the other sentences can support it. Telling readers what the whole text covers is the job of an introduction, not a topic sentence.
a.clue: Think about what one paragraph is mostly about.

b.q: Ravi writes about why his town needs a skate park. His final paragraph opens by saying that, taken as a whole, a skate park would give young people a safe place to meet and be active. Which part of the text is this?
opts: The conclusion, as it draws the ideas together
The introduction, as it says what is coming
A topic sentence, as it opens a body paragraph
A detail, as it supports a main idea
b.why: The sentence sits in the last paragraph and pulls the ideas together, so it belongs to the conclusion. It could be mistaken for a topic sentence because it opens a paragraph, but a topic sentence opens a paragraph that then develops one idea in the body of the text.
b.clue: Look at where the paragraph sits and how it looks back over the whole text.

a.best: It states the main idea of the paragraph

b.best: The conclusion, as it draws the ideas together

problems.detail: The card says a topic sentence 'opens a paragraph and states the main idea of that paragraph' and never limits topic sentences to body paragraphs or explains what a body paragraph is. A student following the card could reasonably think the opening sentence of the final paragraph is also its topic sentence. Only the words 'body paragraph' in that distractor, and the why's appeal to 'the body of the text', rule it out, and the card does not teach that distinction.

b.q: Ravi's text argues that his town needs a skate park. One paragraph is about safety and one is about exercise. Which sentence would best suit his conclusion?
opts: A skate park would keep young people safe and active
A skate park could also bring tourists to our town
This text will explain why our town needs a skate park
Last year, ten students were hurt skating on roads
b.why: This sentence draws together Ravi's two main points, safety and exercise, which is what a conclusion does. The sentence about tourists is tempting because it supports his argument, but it starts a new point, and a conclusion does not do that.
b.clue: Which sentence looks back over points Ravi has already made?

a.best: It states the main idea of the paragraph

b.best: A skate park would keep young people safe and active
